newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy says Albania mission to end August 12.
newsitem.headline: Italy says Albania mission to end August 12.

text.p: Italy on Monday proclaimed the multinational mission it is leading in Albania a success and said troops would withdraw completely by August 12 following elections in the Balkan state in which ex-communist Socialists triumphed.
Defence Chief of Staff Admiral Guido Venturoni, commander of the 7,000-strong security force, said the withdrawal would begin on July 20 and would end within 20 days "if there are no complications".

Speaking to reporters at a book presentation, Venturoni said he expected the troops to be "all out" by August 12 following a controversial mission that once threatened to topple the Italian government.

The 11-nation force began deploying in April to safeguard aid distribution and secure elections held on June 29 and July 6. Albania's victorious Socialist Party look set for a two-thirds parliamentary majority.
"The Multinational Protection Force has managed to restrict organised crime greatly, to keep open communication routes and to get the country moving again," Venturoni said.

The United Nations agreed a 45-day extension of the force's mandate on June 19 after its original term expired on June 28. The extension followed a request from Albania's national unity government, installed to restore political stability in the run-up to elections intended to end months of mayhem.
The elections passed off relatively smoothly in a country that has been under gun rule for months and Venturoni said the security mission had successfully overcome some difficulties.
"We've worked miracles putting together a force with 11 countries, including countries with a strong military tradition such as France," Venturoni said.
"The French don't like being under anyone else's command if they can help it. We've managed to get Turks and Greeks to get along," he added.

However, he said there had been some "resistance" and confusion over the role of the force and questions asked about why it was not disarming Albanians who looted thousands of weapons from state stocks at the height of the unrest.

To have done so could have touched off banditry and street fighting, Venturoni said. "It would have been a worse war than the one in Somalia," he said. Italy was part of a U.N. peacekeeping force sent to the African country.

In a domestic political dispute over deployment of the Albania force, Italy's centre-left coalition was almost toppled in April because of opposition by the Communist Refoundation party to the deployment.
In another bid to normalise the situation in Albania, Italy is seeking to speed up the return of an influx of refugees granted temporary sanctuary at the height of the unrest.

"For every repatriation, by August 31, a contribution of 300,000 lire ($176) has been set to ease reinsertion into Albania," Giulia Falzoi, an official of the Geneva-based International Organisation for Migration (IOM), which will oversee the repatriation, told reporters in Rome on Monday.
"Anyone deciding to return by July 31 will have 200,000 lire extra," she added.

Interior ministry undersecretary Giannicola Sinisi has said those returning early will also be given the chance to qualify for temporary work permits. The plan has sparked outrage from the opposition, which says that would hurt the prospects of unemployed Italians.
